review_text_raw:
The mechanics are that of an uninspired phishing simulation. Which contrasts with the narrative framing of "you are a really dangerous nerd". I feel like a game like grayhack or hacknet is fit more for that framing. Even the tutorial was highly boring for me. Maybe the story you get after the tutorial is good, but i didn't get that far.

Well you see I understand that a game would need some embellishing and effects to sell the power fantasy and divert from the seams of skipping real life logic, but the choices this game made regarding that front makes me see those seams harder rather than immersing me in the fantasy.

very light spoilers ahead from the first ten minutes of gameplay(tutorial and intro)

First, i got whiplashed right off with the phrase "our company got a BILLION BYTES of customer data". Holy shit dude, that's a lot for a large tech company at the like 90s maybe. Not for the presented "everyone is glued to their phones using social media" setting.  Less than a god damn gigabyte, basically three times less than the space this game takes on your ssd.

Then we got the random code prompts opening every time we copy the details from the browser about someone's facebook account to some contacts type information collection software. It feels less hackery and more like the "linux users when x" memes, because why would code prompts open when you are just copy pasting something from one gui to some other gui.


Then apparently we have access to the data of almost all citizens in our nation through the company database software. For some reason when accessing the data we or the software executes almost totally unrelated linux commands, which i don't understand why since it is not a cli tool but poses as a professional corpo gui software, but i guess the company in the story fired the user interface designer/programmer before they finished their job.

Then there is the password "cracker" software. Except this game's version makes me feel like a loser script kiddie the most. All you do is fill in a bunch of details you gathered from the dude's social media page, and the "cracker" spits out some password guess with very few amount of characters based on the entered information. And somehow it's correct like it's some oracle.

It reminds me of that one CheeseParade skit where the guy goes "He's not a hacker, he's a password guesser", and then the guy proceeds to get locked out of the system for inputting the wrong password since it was a guess based on a whim.

Also the OS apparently can't handle a bunch of high speed showcase of cyber security news, crashes and has to restart, which felt like a funny unintentional commentary on the ram shortage crisis. That was the most fun part of the game for me. 

Anyways, so if you like an overly dressed up phishing simulator with seemingly nice worldbuilding and perhaps a good story if you ignore the technical knowledge shortcomings of the writers here and there, maybe its your thing, Otherwise, nah.

review_text_raw:
I played through the first 3 chapters and it's getting pretty repetitive, especially the database searching and cracking functions are pretty much the exact same for all characters. It's kind of a shame that the clue snippet system wasn't better used to let players interact more - any clue snippet that didn't appear under the characters' primary info sections is pretty much useless and only exists to fill the progress bar with very few exceptions. The only clues found that are interactable are basically the name, DOB, email address, etc. Solving parts of the story with the progress bar also felt kind lacking with about 3 mini-puzzles to solve for each one. The writing is okay, but felt kind of generic and easily-guessable, mostly because there are so few characters in each case.

There were a lot of gameplay elements I did not enjoy, for example dialogue scenes like phone calls can't be fast-forwarded (or click to advance faster), and if I make one wrong choice then the whole dialogue has to start from the beginning. What's worse is there are clue snippets to collect after those dialogues and I'm not sure if it was a problem on my end but I couldn't click on them during the scenes, so I was frequently left wondering where the run went wrong. The repetition of the snippet upload animation is also frustrating as it leaves a few seconds where I can't interact with anything while waiting for it to finish.

review_text_raw:
I enjoy mystery/investigation and hacking games, so I was looking forward to trying this one out for a while. That said, I didn't have high expectations going in to this game because it doesn't cost that much. 
However, I wouldn't recommend this game for the following reasons:

1. My choices didn't matter and there was only one correct answer. I was excited to play this because I thought it would have a multi-layered investigation, like "The Roottress are Dead," but it's far short of that. Grabbing data from various documents is the main mechanic, which lead to "inferences," which are mostly guesswork to get the right answer so you can go forward. There were no consequences to getting something wrong, thus no multiple endings.

2. The story lines for the two missions I played were kinda gross to me. [spoiler] Both centered on blond, white women. In the first mission, the woman lied about her domestic abuse and scammed multiple husbands. And in the second the woman was a college student who was forced to be a "sex slave." This trite theme was repulsive to me and not fleshed out in an interesting way.[/spoiler] I quit playing because I lost interest in the overarching story or how the missions were connected.

3. The scripts (and some of the corresponding voice acting) were really bad. They didn't suit the characters at all, so much so that it broke my immersion.

I don't mean to sound cruel, but I'm shocked that is game is so highly rated at the time of my review as it is marred by several critical flaws. 

Most glaringly, the English translation and localisation is atrocious. Considering this is coming from a non-native English speaking studio, I was willing to overlook some of the inaccuracies since there is a lot of text you have to sift through, but even some of the phrases in the "connecting the dots" puzzles, the crux of the game, are unintelligible, and could only solved after looking up the solution. The voice acting is painfully subpar and its apparent that they were not given much direction for their performance. While I don't mind when a game explores dark subject matter, the discovery of the plot is often sapped of any suspense when the villain(s) often brag the same way Dr. Doofenshmirtz does with his evil inventions.

Even if you plan to not play this game in English, I would still recommend avoiding as you will spend the entire game clicking away at every sentence on every site in case it has a meaningful clue to record, as they are the very puzzle pieces you will need to literally connect later. There is more I can say about the game, but I think you get the picture. Instead, consider getting "The Roottrees are Dead" if you want to get your internet sleuth on.

There is a lot to like, but overall I wouldn't _recommend_ this game.

First off, in my perspective, timers ruin most everything that could be fun. Life is busy, interruptions pop up. In this game, one cannot pause and there's not a lot of time allowed for dilly dallying. Always seems a silly way of trying to make something challenging, having to do it faster. The timed parts are simple enough, and seem to be re-doable, but they're not enjoyable that way.  Nearer the end in particular are some puzzles that would be much more enjoyable without a timer or at least with a pause button.

What possibly contributed to souring my experience 
I wound up having to play a bunch of the game over twice, because first I couldn't make any of the boxes on the screen move, during a timed event. After click click clicking all around, I restarted. The game seemed like it was picking up just before the timed part, but nothing I did could trigger the timed part. nothing would happen. So, I restarted from a manual save point. Then, before I caught back up to where I had been, I inadvertently closed a window that then wouldn't open again, and the game proceeded as though I had made a different choice, so I went back to my manual save point again because I didn't want that. Through that experience, I became more aware how tedious the copying and pasting can be.

It’s barely relevant to the information you want t look for.

And the worst part? The game presents obvious clues in fragmented parts, but it doesn’t let you connect them until it decides you’ve "earned it". You can see the bigger picture, but it keeps those pieces hidden, forcing you to waste time hunting for stuff that’s already right in front of you. It’s like the game is deliberately holding back info, making you run in circles just to unlock something that should’ve been obvious from the start.

To top it all off, you can’t even explore anything the game doesn’t deem necessary, no matter how much you know it should be. Even when you’re certain something else is important, the game stops you, forcing you to stick to its narrow path. It’s like being told exactly where to stand and when to look, even though you can see a whole branch of information that just "not related" .

Is this just me being picky about how the game should be or should I try to give it another shot?

review_text_raw:
Cyber Manhunt is a take on an Orwell style game, but it lacks the polish and quality of those titles. Sometimes you can find a piece of information that you need (for example, a character's name) earlier in a chapter, but the game won't let you 'learn' it until you reach a later point because it isn't the specific place where the game wants you to collect that information. Certain dialogue choices are vague and their outcomes are unpredictable. Sometimes the game will ask you to provide specific information that you collected (or information that the game never clearly gave) but won't let you access your 'notes'.

There are a few interesting minigames scattered throughout, but some of them give a strict time limit and vague guidance as to what you need to do. Failure just sets you back a short time, but in some instances you're forced to sit through unskippable dialogue scenes to get back to the minigame.

There are a lot of good ideas here, and the chapters and overall story are fairly interesting, but the overall presentation makes this more of a frustrating experience than a fun one.
